p: I don't have it here currently, but that is something we can follow up with.

Okay, perfect. And then last question is about the vacancy reduction. It's for 40 positions with savings of $9.2 million in FY26, and then $27.6 million in FY '27 and the out years. Um, so it was, you know, disheartening to see these vacancy reductions after years of the council fighting against the previous administration's cuts and vacancy reductions at the Parks Department. We

had hoped for, you know, the one percent, as the Chair mentioned, you know, one percent of the budget to the Parks Department. But this is definitely something that the council included on our side in the preliminary response. And so, has the department decided which specific positions will be reduced? And if so, can you please provide that information?

Sure. You know, I wanna thank again the Council for their continued advocacy for, of course, increasing our budget. We, as the head of an agency, we love talking about bigger budgets and bigger capacity. The truth is, is with these vacancies, we've been under, as you know, the two-for-one hiring freeze for a while. And we see— we've been talking about vacancies for far before this administration. And so the vacancies that we had there were not able to be filled. So we've– it's– you know, we've worked very closely with OMB to have a lot of close conversations about vacancies that are— that we've long had empty versus new ones that are coming up every month and have come up with essentially a plan to move forward with the ability to fill our positions as they become vacant again.

We're very excited about getting rid of the two-for-one piece and really what you're— what, constituents, what our city is feeling right now in terms of our Parks Department, they're not going to really feel any sort of difference in those vacancies because they've been gone for so— they've been gone for quite some time.

And since FY21, I don't know if you have the data for this, but since FY21, how many positions have been reduced as part of the PEGs savings plans, and what level of savings were achieved by the reductions?
I'm sorry, I don't think I have that information available, but I'm happy to—
[interposing] Okay, if you can get back to us.
to follow up with you all.
Okay. And what is the current budgeted and actual headcount for FY26 and '27? And if you could break down the numbers by full-time and part-time, that'd be great.

Sure. So while I flip over to this– our agency full-time budgeted positions for FY27 is 5,141. I do have a historical perspective on that for you as well, but that is significantly up. And then in terms of part-time seasonal positions– oh, sorry, we have around 3,000— yes, full-time equivalent positions, but that results in around roughly 5,000 additional employees, 5,034.
Got it. So 3,000 FTE which equals 5,000.
Yes.
Okay. Perfect. Okay. I have a lot of other questions on trees and everything else, but you know what, I am going to pass it off to our Chair Hankerson.

Thank you, Chair. Just a few questions. Just going back to the one-shots. Can you please provide a breakdown of the remaining one-shots that were not included in the Executive Plan along with their funding amounts in FY26 and any supported headcount?

Sure. So, of the remaining one-shots that are still up for question,

we have– there are three real buckets. There's our Parks Enforcement Patrol, our Green Thumb program, and stump removal funds, which we're very grateful for. I'll take them in backwards order. So for stump removal, it's approximately $2 million of stump removal. This is has not yet been baselined. It also complements $1.4 million— or last year it complemented $1.4 million of mayoral baseline funding in FY26, $3.4 million total. The number of stumps that comes out to kind of depends year-to-year based on the type of stump and removal kind of period. But it’s roughly between 4,000 to 5,500 removals per year. In addition to that, our Green Thumb program, the one-shot funding was in FY26 $2.6 million. That results— that really equates to 15 positions with additional funding for OTPS. Our Green Thumb program is around– is 32 baseline year-round lines. And so these 15 additional positions do represent a significant portion of our workforce there. And I'm happy to talk more about the Green Thumb program and what that does. The one-shot fund— the OTPS funding for this program also goes to tree pruning and

removal— tree removals within the Green Thumb community gardens.
I appreciate that. Let's just say—
[interposing] Would you like me to talk about the PEP?
No, not yet.
Okay.

Let's just say PEP or Green Thumb, you know, don't receive funding in the adopted budget. What will Parks do with those employees who will no longer have jobs? Will they be given jobs elsewhere in the agency or the city? Will they receive severance checks? What's the plan?

Yeah, we would typically in that case, which we hope is not the case, we would typically work with each of these individuals to see if they would be eligible to be moved into other open lines or any grant-funded lines. We have unfortunately seen this happen in the past where programs or portions of our departments are not funded in another year. And so we work very hard to try to ensure that as many of our staff that

can be accommodated in other portions of our agency can do so. It's of course though based on availability of open lines and positions.
So if there are no open lines or positions, what happens to them?
Then their lines are only funded until the end of the fiscal year.
They would be without a job?
Yes.
Just to be clear. Okay. Will all baseline positions be filled by those who are currently employed in those roles, or will they be open to the public to be filled?
I'm sorry, can you repeat that question one more time?
So, will all baseline positions be filled by those who are currently employed, or are you opening it up to the public to apply?

Sorry. Yes, yes, by and large, unless there's some, like, disciplinary infraction that is pending, which I don't know of any

right now. Yes, all the positions would be filled by those who have them now.
Will Parks continue to push for expanded positions in those areas, or do you feel that you have the adequate amount with the current numbers?

Sure, as I've said before, more is always more. In leading our agency, we are very thrilled to have the positions that we have. We're really excited about these $15 million of baseline positions. Again, historic and very, very promising and a real indication of our value within the city. But of course, we'd always welcome more resources whenever available.
The plan included an additional $7.9 million beginning in FY27 for recreation staff. Which centers will those— will these staff be stationed at? Can you provide a breakdown by title?

Sure. We are happy to give you a breakdown of title, but at a later date for a couple reasons. The plan is— the plan is funding three different recreation centers:

Owen Dolen, St. Mary's, and Mary Cali Dalton. Mary Cali Dalton is still being built, so we won't be actually hiring until closer to when it's opening up. And St. Mary's and Owen Dolen, same thing. We'd be hiring a little bit closer to when these are opening up. They're all opening up very soon this year, which we're really excited about. There are a number of lines when it comes to management– recreation centers. We have center managers, deputy center managers, CPWs, recreation associates, PEP officers, lifeguards, sometimes IT folks who are there. So there's a number of different titles that we have, sometimes resident engineers, depending for new buildings, like Shirley Chisholm and others. So we're happy to give you that information as it becomes available. We'll be making those decisions closer to when we're hiring so that we can really see how, particularly for those two rec centers that are reopening, how that balances out with our existing staff.
Is it the practice of Parks to hire from the local community that the rec center is in or being built in?

I mean, we'd certainly try to as much possible. I think that we have— I'm very proud of my agency's relationship and how we engage with local communities. I think it's really important. I think that we should be continuing to not just rest on our laurels, but push ourselves further and harder to make sure that we are truly community-based entities and an agency that's rooted in the communities that we are very proud and privileged to serve in. So, certainly with Shirley Chisholm, which is my first big recreation center opening, our first big one in the last 10 years. We're very proud to be working hand in hand with the community. I think our center manager is actually from East Flatbush, if I recall correctly. Not that that's always a mandatory piece, but we're always looking for opportunities to engage more local New Yorkers.
We're also excited about the center that's coming to our Deputy Speaker's District very soon as well.
Yes.
So looking forward to that.
Groundbreaking this year.
This year? She said it, not me. Are there any additional part-time staff that will be hired along with the staff that are currently at the centers?
No, what we have presented to us in the— in this year's executive budget is what we'll be hiring for.
How long does the agency believe it will take to fully hire these positions?
I don't think it takes very long. We— this is something that we are very good at doing. We will start, I believe as soon as the new fiscal year begins, as we get closer to these openings.

Just to jump over to capital projects, Parks has one of the largest capital budgets of any department, $3.9 billion between FY26 and 2030. Yet it consistently has long

project timelines and issues with delays, to which I know all my colleagues can probably speak to. I've seen this firsthand in my district with police at— Police Officer Edward Byrne Park, to which comfort stations were funded by my predecessor's predecessor, and construction is finally starting next month. Sorry, July. What is the current budgeted and actual headcount for the Capital Projects Division?
Sure. So our budgeted headcount for capital is approximately 400— I'm just looking this up to make sure— 450 staffers. Sorry, I'm– and then I think that our actual headcount is 390 with 60 vacancies.
390 with 60 vacancies? Are there any issues with hiring capital analysts, engineers, project managers, or architects?

You know, I wouldn't say issues, but there are certainly unique challenges of hiring for these– of hiring for these specific positions. Most importantly, that we are competing with the private industry when it comes to these roles. They are highly specialized and oftentimes even competing with other agencies for the

same type of— for very simple similar and– positions. I'd say that we're looking very closely at this. I would like to see this division completely staffed, staffed up and looking very closely at how, to your first point, we can shave down the time of these capital projects. I completely agree with you. I think that our capital timeline— I understand the length of time, but I also think it is far too long. And so however we can work together, and we are talking to our sister agencies on this because a lot of it does come back to regulatory responsibilities that we have in meeting other rules pieces of laws. We're going to look very collaboratively at how we shave this timeline down.

Sure. Is there anything that you could suggest since, you know, we're here and I believe most members, if not all of them on this dais, have the same issues when it comes to timeline with capital projects. Is there anything the council can do? Do you have any suggestions for us?

Yeah, I really appreciate the question. You know, I think that what—

there are a few things. One is that we really should and would love to have an ongoing conversation with you about pieces of legislation that could be moved along. There are pieces of legislation in past administrations, past members of the Council who have talked about various kind of efforts that could potentially shorten this timeline down. Without getting in– too into the weeds, something like suggesting that a vendor gets registered with MOCS once as a vendor, but not necessarily specifically for every project could maybe close–, could shorten timelines for registration or things like that. We're working with our sister agency, DEP, as well as OTI right now under my leadership with Commissioner Garcia and others to look at the SWIP process, which we know has significantly added to our timeframe, both in time but also in cost, looking at ways that we can shorten down that, be it through rule changes or just through maybe even having staffing from different agencies sit within our own agencies so that we can streamline these processes. We'll happily report to you more on that. I'd also say that a lot of times we see our projects expand in timeline

because we see a lot of kind of scope creep in these things. We see a lot of times scope kind of expanding projects. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but it does complicate the overall procurement design processes and other things like that. And in large part, I'd say that's a good thing because we also— it's because we are rooted in community input. We start every capital project with community input. I think we're the only agency that does so. And that also means that because we have– many times where we're going back to the community, we are adjusting our design designs every time, and that also can just add to the timeline. One ask I would say is that just working in close collaboration with your borough commissioners and with our capital team would be very helpful because we can help in collaboration together direct, like, you on projects that we know are just over the— just there to get fully funded, or that have, like, some other ways that we can group these projects together to kind of move the needle forward kind of faster. So I'd say close working relationships, which we're very grateful for already with our council members and the capital team, is a

big piece. Happy to talk to you more about other pieces of legislation, and then we'll be continuing to come back to you to discuss ways that we are specifically trying to shorten the SWIP process.

Thank you. I do want to acknowledge we've been joined by Council Members Nurse, Hudson, P. Sanchez, Wong, and on Zoom we have Council Members Ung and Brooks-Powers. I just have a couple more questions. I'm going to turn over to my colleagues, and then I'll circle back again with some more questions. The admin has gone back to the baseline. The admin has not baselined 100 PEP officers who are on expiring contracts. Roughly what percentage of the total PEP do these 100 positions represent? Would you say these positions are critical to the agency?

Yes, absolutely. Our PEP officers, as anyone who is in our parks know, are absolutely critical components to our agency. They are peace officers first and foremost, but they also have an extraordinarily difficult job that they do very well every day. They are there to essentially enforce our rules. And it's never fun to go up to a

stranger and tell them that they're not following a rule or that they need to do something differently. But that's what our officers do. They also educate the public on all things around our parks and making the spaces welcoming for everyone. They represent the 100 officers that are— that were in one-shot funding represent a strong component of our overall number we have 350— roughly 354 officer lines and this is including those 100 officers.
Do they specialize in conflict resolution?
Absolutely, yes. So we train— they go through rigorous training for, I believe it's 16 weeks, and much of that is in conflict resolution.
Would you say that without them, we may see an increase in crime in parks?
I'd say that PEP Officers are one of our best tools to enforce rules, can keep people safe and engaged in our parks in appropriate ways.
Thank you. The admin has not baselined 15 positions for Green Thumb. What do these particular roles do, and how many community gardens does Green Thumb serve?

I believe, and I will double-check, our Green Thumb program has around 500 gardens in our entire portfolio, although I can get that number confirmed for you. Our– as I mentioned before, the 15 green staff lines represent again a significant number of our overall unit of– they are 15 and then plus another 32, so 47 total. Our Green Thumb program is incredibly important and a very, like, a very just culturally significant program because they allow for everyday New Yorkers to have a very different type of relationship with the land and with our park system. It's through our Green Fund program that families that New York residents are able to cultivate the land. They are able to create spaces for their communities that celebrate community— the differences in our communities, that celebrate the diversity of our communities, and have been oftentimes created when it feels like the surrounding neighborhood was just in

so many ways falling apart, and it's these gardens that have turned communities around. They've really kind of become pillars in every neighborhood that they are in. So they are significant. They provide tremendous benefit way beyond— they punch before— above their weight, I would say, in terms of what they bring back to their communities. And every single one of those staff members is incredibly vital to our agency.
I just have two more questions and then I'll circle back. Where would you, Commissioner, like to see additional positions if additional one-shots were funded by this Council?

Thank you for the question. I– as the leader of this agency, I don't necessarily like choosing between my children, so I will defer on that, but I'd say that there's not one corner of my agency that is not being used to its full capacity. We provide incredibly wide range of programs and services. It's a very— you've heard me in my testimony talk about 30,000 acres of parkland, 14 miles of beaches, and reading up about this, we have 160 miles of coastline in our city that we

actually are taking care of in our wetlands, our 160 acres— sorry, not miles, 160 acres of coastlines that we're caring for in terms of our natural areas as well. There's not one division of my agency that's not absolutely serving New York and delivering on a very full, rich, and diverse public realm. So I, of course, would welcome additional resources in any component of that. I'm, you know, happy to talk about specifically these one-shot positions or the other historical positions that were one-shot previously and now baselined. But every department I'm extraordinarily proud of and can make a very strong argument that they are absolutely essential to our agency.
Thank you. My final question. The Mayor campaigned on a promise to get parks to one percent. What is the plan? Yeah.

Well, happy— I, you know, I certainly was very enthusiastic, very excited to hear that same– that same promise of the one percent. I think that what I'd say is that we are in constant communication with the Mayor truly, even as earlier today and every day we are talking about

what it looks like to expand parks budget. We were talking about what the real felt experience of what that looks like on the ground. I'm extremely grateful for our advocates and partners in this because we are in regular communication about not only what one percent means, but what it means to expand staffing across the board and what that will feel like when we're able to achieve that. In the meantime, I'd say that our plan is always the same, to deliver high— the highest quality public realm possible to all New Yorkers, regardless of who they are, with the resources that we're given.
Do you think we'll get there?
I hope— I, yeah. Yes, I do.
Okay. Thank you, Commissioner. I'm going to turn it over to our colleagues.

Great. So also want to recognize we have been joined by Majority Leader Abreu, as well as Council Member Krishnan. And we

will start with our Deputy Speaker, followed by Council Member Brewer.
Hello. I just had a few questions. I'm going to be a little bit all over the place, but the permit division— can you share how many people work in the citywide permit division?

I'm not sure. One— if you don't mind, one moment. I may ask our Assistant Commissioner David Cerron to join us to give the specifics on our permit division. But while he's coming up, I'd say that our permit division is divided kind of in twofold. We have our borough permit offices, which handle everything from your average birthday party to, I'd say, kind of more run-of-the-mill events. When it comes to specialized, kind of citywide or specialized permitting, be it large-scale events or permitting that has special elements to it, commercial elements to it, or otherwise just big events, that goes to our citywide permitting office, which I think is probably what you're asking about.
I'm 100 percent talking about citywide.
Okay, so I'll turn to David Cerron then to—
Borough permits office is not the problem.
Great.
As you know.
Good afternoon. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?
I do.
You may begin.
It's nine, council member. Thank you for the question.
And how many permit requests get funneled to the citywide division every year?
They're processing approximately 1,000.
Do you think that is an adequate amount of staff to process 1,000 permit requests every year?

We're happy to work with the resources that we have. Of course, it's always helpful to have more resources, like, you know, every city agency, but we're going to continue to do the best with the team that we have.

Okay. A question about the PEP officers in Roy Wilkins. So I know when my predecessor fought really hard to, like, baseline about $1 million to Roy Wilkins, the PEP officers were specifically for Roy Wilkins, but as I understand it, the PEP officers are moving around multiple parks in Southeast Queens. And as you know, we had the tragedy a month or so ago. And I love my Queens Borough Commissioner, and I understand the thinking around having the PEP officers move around, considering there may not be a lot of activity in one particular park, but considering that Roy Wilkins specifically has a very large volume of young people that go after school in the summer, I just wanted to know if the Parks Department was thinking about

increasing the number of PEP officers in Southeast Queens so that they don't have to rotate? Obviously, prior to my predecessor, I don't think there were any PEP officers in our area. So I just wanted to understand the thinking around that, how many PEP officers are assigned to Roy Wilkins?

Sure. So thank you for the question. So certainly we can look at this. We, of course, we're— we have our 350-ish, 354 officers for the entire city. When it comes to– we try to cover as much ground as humanly possible when it comes to that specific funding. Happy to look into this and, and to see. We know how important Roy Wilkins is. We know how heavily used it is throughout really every season, but particularly during the summertime. So happy to look at that. And in terms of overall staffing numbers, we are constantly trying to take a data-driven approach as much as possible towards deploying our staff, trying to cover our hotspots, our spots where we know a lot of people are going. We also, of course, during the summertime are extending our PEP officers also then to beaches and

pools as well. So we just cut— try to cover as much ground as we can, but we'll certainly—

[interposing] Yeah, and in Southeast Queens, we're always one big happy family. And so for me, it's fine to have the PEP officers rotate between Council Member Hankerson's district and mine. But what I don't want to see is that the resources that were technically supposed to be for one particular park get stretched thin, versus your department deciding to just invest a little bit more in Southeast Queens. Like, that money was for Roy Wilkins and for the PEP officers in Roy Wilkins, which again, I think it's fine for us to share, especially if the activity is not as much in certain parks, but I just want you all to review that and not, like, continue to use the PEP officers that technically were not for other parks.
Sure.

I have just one more question, and then I guess I'll come back for round two, Chair. Okay, so the other question I have is I know I spoke to you— I can't remember the name of the title of the rec staff that technically

technically– which I didn't even know this existed, but that does the pickup play games in the park?
Playground Associates.

Playground Associates, yes. Can you just share how many Playground Associates exist across the city? Because I've never heard of that position. I don't think there's any Playground Associates in Southeast Queens, but prove me wrong. But yeah, I just– I think that is a low-key equity issue, because I don't think—
I would love to know where the Playground Associates are and if they are, like, equally distributed across New York City.

Sure. I'm going to look to our Deputy Commissioner Margaret Nelson to give us a little more information, but while she's coming up, I'm happy to talk a little bit more. So, the program that I think you're referring to is our Playground Associate Program. It's the same group of people who are also helping staff our summer camp program, but we have— I think last summer we had 73

playground associates that we put— you'll see them in yellow shirts, they should be wearing yellow shirts, and they are stationed throughout parks throughout the city. And we will definitely get you a list of where they are located. I don't know if we've actually come up with— oh, we did come up with a list of locations– oh, by borough. We can give you that list by borough, but we can also give you a list by park after this.
Yes, I would look—
We have 23–
[interposing] How many parks do we have?
Of course we have we have thousands.
Yes, and we only have 73 playground associates.

Yeah, so we do them strategically. We pick the locations where, of course, there's a public restroom building, of course, where there's some sort of, like, water play, and then we– where we know that we're able to reach

as many kids as possible. It's an incredible program, and I'm grateful for your question because it gives me an opportunity to talk about it in more detail. But we know that oftentimes, and I was one of those kids, where you work dur— your mom– your parents work during the summertime and you just have no place to go. So you either hang out at home in the apartment or you go out in the parks by yourself. And we know that for many kids, parents, myself included, it's a terrifying idea to have your kids go out there without any sort of adult presence. Our Playground Associates create that adult presence. They are there to engage kids in any sort of activity. They're there to make sure that they're drinking water, that they're cooling down. It's board games, it's basketball, it's playing on the— it's playing– doing– kicking a ball around on a soccer field. It's all of these things and more. They're out there keeping an eye out and looking for kids. And I'm sure Margaret can give you some of the numbers, but when it comes to how many kids we're actually reading, the number— while it is a small program of 73 playground associates, we’re reaching thousands, if not tens of

thousands of kids every summer, and it's tremendous. I want more families to know about this program. I'm really enthusiastic about it. It is a tough job to be out there all day just looking out for kids, but that's what we do. It is meant to complement the– a number of other very affordable opportunities that we provide to New Yorkers. I believe that this is like a network of services that is absolutely our job to provide, and I'm very proud of what this program brings. Margaret can give you some of the more specific numbers.
Good afternoon. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before the committee, and to respond honestly to committee questions?
I do.
You may begin.

Thank you. I think you summarized it, you know, amazingly, but just to give you some of the numbers, we do have 73 sites currently, and that's pretty much been our historic average for the past couple years. We have 13 sites in the Bronx, 14 in Brooklyn, 23 in Queens,

13 in Manhattan, and 10 in Staten Island. And I don't have the list of the exact parks, but we can get that to you, in terms of especially Southeast Queens. And then in 2025 we served over 440,000 participants during the summer. And that is a big increase from 2024 where we served approximately 300,000. And I would also just like to add, in addition to what our commissioner said, you know, these are seasonal positions. So we are recruiting people with some experience working with kids, and they are out in those playgrounds every day working with these kids. And if you can do that job, we're like, you should be in recreation. And so it is a good pipeline for us too, to hire folks from the community, work with our kids students in the summer, and then when we have positions available, kind of bring them into our full-time workforce.
Thank you, and I appreciate all the details, and I would love to just see it expanded, because I agree that it's a good program and nobody knows that it exists.
Alright, thank you. And we have you down for round two. Council Member Brewer followed by Council Member Narcisse.

Thank you very much, and congratulations, Commissioner, on your hard work. I am aware of your hard work and it's showing. Thank you. On the PEP officers, what— I know you have 354, 100 hopefully will get included in that– there are included. How many do you really need?

I mean, right now our PEP officers are— thank you for the question and thank you for your comments. Right now our PEP officers are predominantly running on, as the Deputy Speaker mentioned, really trying to cover as much ground as we possibly can. There are situations where we have them be stationary in parks, but we're trying to cover as much ground as possible. I'd say again, we'd welcome as many resources as possible. We know the benefit of PEP officers here. It would be lovely to see as many— we'd see— we'd love a presence in the—

[interposing] Even Central Park needs them. They have their own ranger

corps, but between the e-bikes and the $42 million people and other parks similarly, you need more PEP officers. So at some point, I think you should tell us how many you need, and then we should be advocating for that. Just a suggestion. Number two, trees. You know, I hate your program. Yes. So my question is, how much— because we're never going to get another freaking tree in Manhattan. So my question is, how much does it cost? Maybe you answered this.
Yes.

I didn't hear an answer. Per tree, if you're— I know if it costs you in-house, $2,900. I got that. But I have— I can't use you. So what's— where else can I— where do I go? Do I go to New York Trees? Do I get— do I— can somebody just put a tree in the the pot, in the pit? How do I get more? How does that work?
Yeah, thank you for— we did answer your question, but we're happy to talk about this, and thank you. I—
[interposing] Well, you didn't say how else I can get a tree.

So you can— there are a couple ways. So constituents or anybody, yourself included can plant– purchase their own tree, and they could work with us. We can help give directions on the type of tree to plant, any sort of planting guidelines. We do like to advise on types of trees that are–
[interposing] I understand that.

you know, here and complementary to the trees that we have. They can also go to Tree Time, which is our partner in this, a and that kind of fast-tracks also trees being put in plant— in tree beds, and then, I'd say that those are the two primary ways. I'd also say though that in terms of the work that we're doing, of course, I would remind you that it's not just about planting trees, but it's also removing stumps, and then covering up tree pits that are no longer viable trees.

I know. I just want more trees. They're dying like crazy. And so I guess what you're— I mean, I'm still trying to get

rid of your program and find another program, a complementary program, something. I have the same question. You need X number of PEP officers, but how much do you need to actually have a real tree planting program that would plant 1,800 in every neighborhood or whatever is needed?

Yeah, thank you. I mean, I think our forestry– in terms of our street trees that we have and that we care for, and including also the landscaped parks are around 880,000 trees. So it's a tremendous amount of trees that we're caring for, and are— we're able to care for that many trees through a combination of contracted work and in our in-house unit.
Okay. And lifeguards— now, I don't want— are they out of Chelsea? I mean, out of 60th Street Rec Center? And how— thanks to Iris, lifeguards are increasing.
Yes.
I give her full credit. So my question is, do you have enough for the summer? Can you move them out? Are they moved out of– what's the name of that stupid thing that Adrienne—
[interposing] [inaudible] Gertrude [sic].
Yeah, I hate that name. That was Adrienne's idea. The 60th Street Rec Center. Are they out of there?

No, we're still— we're— so our lifeguard— so thank you. We are still certifying, recertifying, and recertifying our lifeguards. I'll turn to our First Deputy Commissioner to give us more information about this. We'll be continuing to do this and get them all trained and get them out into our beaches and pools. Up through the Fourth of July is where we'll hit— we'll hit our peak. We right now are looking very good at our numbers. We're higher this year at this point in time than we were last year.
